back: Appraisal: broad term including surveys, interviews, observations, and tests. Test: instrument that measures a sample of behavior (assigns a number/score). Psychometrics: the branch of counseling/psychology focused on psychological measurement; practitioner = psychometrician.
confusable_with: Assessment and evaluation are synonyms for appraisal on the exam

back: Subjective: scorer's opinion/judgment heavily influences scoring (essays, projectives). Objective: rater's judgment plays little or no part (forced-choice, multiple-choice). NCE and CPCE are objective tests. Halo effect is a risk in subjective scoring.
confusable_with: Projective tests use free-response (subjective format) but the 'projection' refers to the client's personality, not the scoring method

front: Forced choice (recognition) vs. free choice items
back: Forced choice: examinee selects from 2+ alternatives (MCQ, true/false). Used to control social desirability (MMPI-2 lie scale). Dichotomous = 2 options (true/false); Multipoint = 3+ options (NCE). Free choice (free response): examinee responds any way; more info but harder to score, increases subjectivity.
confusable_with: Ipsative measures often use forced-choice format, but ipsative refers to how scores are interpreted, not format type

back: Normative: individual's score compared to a norm group (percentile rank). Ipsative: traits compared within the same individual; cannot legitimately compare two people's ipsative scores. Kuder career instruments are classic examples of ipsative measures. Within-person analysis = ipsative.
confusable_with: Ipsative scores look like normal scores but you CANNOT compare individuals — only compare the person to themselves

front: Speed test vs. power test vs. timed test
back: Speed test: easy items, time-limited; designed so no one finishes; difficulty from time pressure, not item difficulty. Power test: no time limit; evaluates level of mastery; ideally no one gets a perfect score. Timed test: has time limit but most finish; more difficult items (e.g., NCE, CPCE = timed test).
confusable_with: NCE/CPCE are timed tests, NOT speed tests — most examinees finish; speed tests are designed so no one finishes

back: Spiral: items get progressively more difficult throughout the entire test. Cyclical: multiple sections, each section is spiral (each section goes from easier to harder, then resets).
confusable_with: Both involve difficulty variation, but spiral is one continuous progression while cyclical resets across sections

front: Test battery vs. vertical test vs. horizontal test
back: Test battery: multiple measures combined for more accurate results than any single test alone. Vertical test: different versions for different age/education levels (e.g., math achievement for preschoolers vs. middle school). Horizontal test: measures multiple factors in a single testing session.
confusable_with: Group vs. individual format is not the same as horizontal vs. vertical — these describe content structure

front: Validity — definition and the 5 main types
back: Validity: does the test measure what it claims to measure? Most important test quality. Five types: (1) Content/rational/logical — samples the behavior domain; (2) Construct — measures an abstract trait; (3) Concurrent — compares to established tests; (4) Predictive/empirical — forecasts future behavior; (5) Consequential — social implications of test use. Criterion validity = concurrent + predictive combined.
confusable_with: Face validity (how test 'looks') is NOT one of the five main types; it is not technically valid as a validity measure

back: Whether the test adequately samples the full domain of behavior being measured. Also called rational or logical validity. Example: an IQ test that only measures memory but not vocabulary, math, etc. has poor content validity — a savant might score higher than a broadly gifted person.
confusable_with: Content validity is about breadth of sampling; construct validity is about measuring the theoretical concept itself

back: The extent a test measures an abstract psychological trait or theoretical construct (e.g., ego strength, intelligence, self-esteem, artistic talent, mechanical ability). Any trait that cannot be directly observed/measured is a construct. Theory-based tests (e.g., MBTI based on Jungian theory) claim strong construct validity.
confusable_with: Content validity (sampling domain) vs. construct validity (measuring theoretical concept) — both relate to what is measured, but differently

front: Concurrent vs. predictive validity (both = criterion validity)
back: Criterion validity: the test is evaluated against an external criterion. Two subtypes: Concurrent validity — how well the test compares to other established instruments measuring the same thing NOW. Predictive validity (empirical validity) — how well the test forecasts future behavior/performance (e.g., GRE predicts grad school success). Both types use correlation coefficients; closer to 1.00 = better.
confusable_with: Concurrent = comparing to other tests NOW; predictive = forecasting FUTURE behavior — exam scenarios about 'predicting job performance' = predictive

back: Both are methods for assessing construct/criterion validity. Convergent validity: test correlates with related/similar measures (as expected). Discriminant validity: test does NOT correlate with unrelated variables (near-zero correlation). Example: phobia test should correlate with panic responses (convergent) but NOT with IQ (discriminant).
confusable_with: Convergent ≠ concurrent — convergent compares to related variables; concurrent compares to other tests for the same thing

back: Incremental validity: (1) test becomes more valid as contradictory items are dropped; (2) test provides additional valid information beyond what other measures provide. Synthetic validity: I/O psychology approach for small firms — identify tests that predict each job component separately, then combine them to improve selection.
confusable_with: Neither is one of the main 5 types of validity but may appear on advanced questions

back: Reliability: consistency of measurement across repeated administrations. Second most important test quality (validity is #1). KEY RULES: A valid test is ALWAYS reliable. A reliable test is NOT always valid. Reliability places a ceiling on validity but validity does not set limits on reliability.
confusable_with: Students often confuse which direction the ceiling applies — reliability caps validity; high reliability doesn't guarantee validity

back: (1) Test-retest: same test, same group, two administrations (≥7 days apart); measures stability; best for stable traits like IQ. (2) Equivalent/alternate forms: parallel forms given to same group; counterbalancing needed. (3) Split-half: divide test into even vs. odd items, correlate halves; corrected by Spearman-Brown formula. (4) Inter-rater/inter-observer (scorer reliability): multiple raters assess same response; used with projectives and essay tests.
confusable_with: Split-half is a type of internal consistency reliability, as are KR-20/KR-21 and Cronbach's alpha — but split-half divides the test in half

back: Kuder-Richardson formulas (KR-20, KR-21): measure internal consistency (inter-item consistency/homogeneity) — whether all items measure the same construct — WITHOUT splitting the test in half. Cronbach's alpha: similar alternative statistic. Both are alternatives to the split-half method.
confusable_with: KR-20 does NOT split the test in half — it measures internal consistency using all items simultaneously; split-half divides the test

front: Reliability coefficient benchmarks and coefficient of determination
back: Reliability coefficients: 1.00 = perfect (only physical measurements). .90 = excellent for counseling/psychological tests. .80 = minimum for job/school selection. .70 = typical/acceptable for most personality tests. Coefficient of determination: r² — square the correlation to get the percentage of shared variance. Example: r = .70 → .70² = .49 = 49% true variance, 51% error.
confusable_with: Reliability coefficient ≠ percentage of people who score accurately — it reflects % of score attributable to true variance vs. error

back: SEM: estimates how much a score fluctuates due to random error if the same person took the test repeatedly. Lower SEM = higher reliability. Formula used: X = T + E (obtained score = true score + error). SEM defines confidence intervals: 68% CI = obtained score ± 1 SEM. Example: score of 106, SEM = 3 → 68% CI is 103–109.
confusable_with: SEM is NOT the same as standard deviation of a norm group — SEM reflects individual score error, not population spread

front: Spearman-Brown formula and effect of test length on reliability
back: Spearman-Brown formula: estimates the effect of lengthening or shortening a test on its reliability coefficient. Longer test = higher reliability; shorter test = lower reliability. Used to correct the split-half reliability coefficient (since splitting halves the test length).
confusable_with: Spearman-Brown is about test length adjustments — NOT to be confused with Spearman's two-factor theory of intelligence

back: Cross-validation: administering a test to a NEW sample to confirm that the original validity coefficient holds up. Necessary when original sample is small. Shrinkage: the cross-validation coefficient is typically SMALLER than the original validity coefficient — this is expected and does not mean the test is flawed.
confusable_with: Cross-validation checks validity generalizability; it is NOT the same as test-retest reliability

back: Sir Francis Galton (England): intelligence is a single unitary factor, primarily genetic; exceptional ability runs in families. Book: Hereditary Genius (1869). Believed intelligence related to sensory acuity and reaction time. Half-cousin of Darwin. Associated with the eugenics movement.
confusable_with: Galton (unitary factor) vs. Spearman (two-factor G+S) vs. Guilford (120 factors) — all studied intelligence structure

back: Charles Spearman (1904): proposed two factors — G (general intelligence, applicable to any mental task) and S (specific ability, applicable to a particular task). G is the most important and is shared across all cognitive tasks.
confusable_with: Spearman (G and S factors) vs. Guilford (120 factors) vs. Cattell (fluid and crystallized)

back: J.P. Guilford: used factor analysis to isolate 120 factors (abilities) that comprise intelligence. Famous for distinguishing convergent thinking (combining diverse ideas into one answer) vs. divergent thinking (generating novel, multiple ideas/solutions — creativity).
confusable_with: Convergent and discriminant are validity terms; convergent and divergent thinking are Guilford's intelligence concepts — don't mix

back: Raymond B. Cattell: Fluid intelligence — inherited neurological capacity; flexible, culture-free, content-free reasoning; decreases with age (e.g., block design, pictorial analogies). Crystallized intelligence — built from education, culture, and experience; measured by content-based tests; remains stable or grows with age.
confusable_with: James McKeen Cattell (coined 'mental test') ≠ Raymond B. Cattell (fluid/crystallized; 16 PF)

back: Alfred Binet + Theodore Simon: created first intelligence test in 1905 (Paris). Purpose: identify children with intellectual disabilities for separate schooling. 30-item test with school-related items of increasing difficulty. Based on concept that intelligence = ability to understand school-related material. A 9-year-old task = one that 50% of 9-year-olds answer correctly.
confusable_with: Simon-Binet created for children with ID, not for gifted assessment — Stanford-Binet is the Americanized version by Terman

front: IQ formula — ratio IQ vs. deviation IQ
back: Original ratio IQ formula (by William Stern, German): MA/CA × 100 (mental age divided by chronological age × 100). Memory: MA is a high degree, so it goes on top. Now replaced by deviation IQ: compares individual to age-peer norm group. Stanford-Binet today uses Standard Age Score (SAS): mean = 100, SD = 16.
confusable_with: Binet created the test; Stern created the IQ formula; Terman Americanized it — three different people

back: Lewis Terman (Stanford University): translated and adapted the Binet for American children in 1916 after testing ~3,000 U.S. children. Named it the Stanford-Binet. Current Stanford-Binet 5 (SB5): mean = 100, SD = 16; measures IQ from very low to 180 (wider range than Wechsler); standardized/individual test.
confusable_with: Terman Americanized the Binet; Binet created the original; Wechsler created his own separate IQ tests

back: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV: ages 16–90 years; mean = 100, SD = 15; takes 60–90 min; 10 subtests (subtest mean = 10, SD = 3); measures IQ 40–160. Four indexes: VCI (verbal comprehension), PRI (perceptual reasoning), WMI (working memory), PSI (processing speed). FSIQ = Full Scale IQ. Based on Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory. Can be administered online.
confusable_with: WAIS-IV no longer provides separate Verbal IQ and Performance IQ scores — it provides four index scores instead

front: Wechsler age ranges: WPPSI-IV, WISC-IV, WAIS-IV
back: WPPSI-IV (Preschool/Primary): ages 2 years 6 months to 7 years 7 months. WISC-IV (Children): ages 6 to 16 years 11 months. WAIS-IV (Adult): ages 16 to 90 years. All have mean = 100, SD = 15. Stanford-Binet is better for extremes of intellect (IQ range up to 180); Wechsler good for average range.
confusable_with: WPPSI vs. WISC overlap at age 6–7 — use WPPSI-IV below ~7.5; use WISC-IV above 6

front: Army Alpha and Army Beta — WWI group testing
back: WWI sparked the group IQ testing movement. Army Alpha: for literate English-speaking recruits. Army Beta: for illiterates and non-English speakers (nonverbal/pictorial). ~2 million men tested. Led to widespread adoption of group testing in schools, government, and industry. Group tests: cheaper and faster but less accurate and lower reliability than individual tests.
confusable_with: Army Alpha = literates; Army Beta = illiterates — these are verbal vs. nonverbal, not better vs. worse

front: Culture-fair testing and ethics of test use with diverse populations
back: Culture-fair test: attempts to remove items that are only known due to cultural background. Most experts believe a truly 'culture-free' test does not exist. Key ethics rule: It is unethical to administer a test to a client unless the test has been normed on that specific population. Administering an unvalidated test to a minority group = ethics violation.
confusable_with: Culture-fair ≠ culture-free — culture-fair tries to reduce bias; culture-free claims no cultural influence (theoretically impossible)

back: Arthur Jensen (1969, Harvard Educational Review): article 'How Much Can We Boost IQ and Scholastic Performance?' Claimed IQ is 80% heredity, 20% environment; that White Americans score 11–15 IQ points higher than African Americans regardless of social class, potentially due to selective breeding during slavery. Sparked major controversy. Bronfenbrenner challenged Jensen's twin studies' internal validity.
confusable_with: Jensen's claim of heredity at 80% is the exam stat — contrast with others who said heredity <50%

front: Robert Williams and BITCH test / Larry P. v. Wilson Riles
back: Robert Williams: African American psychologist; created BITCH (Black Intelligence Test of Cultural Homogeneity) to demonstrate that African Americans excel on culturally relevant tests; charged Binet/Wechsler represent 'scientific racism.' Larry P. v. Wilson Riles (1979, California): court ruled IQ tests (Wechsler/Binet) were racially biased against African Americans, who were overrepresented in EMR (educable mentally retarded) classes based on IQ scores.
confusable_with: BITCH = cultural critique test by Williams; Larry P. = landmark legal case; both challenge bias in IQ tests but are different events

back: Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory-2: 567 true/false/'cannot say' items; for ages 18+; 6th grade reading level; 60–90 min; developed 1940, revised 1989; 'gold standard' in personality testing; most researched test in history; self-report; uses lie scale (forced-choice items) to detect social desirability/faking. MMPI-A: 478 items for ages 14–18.
confusable_with: MMPI-2 is a self-report (not projective) personality test despite being considered comprehensive — projectives use ambiguous stimuli

back: 16 PF (Raymond B. Cattell): factor-analytic personality test; ages 16+; measures 16 personality factors (e.g., assertiveness, emotional maturity); can be used for marital counseling. MBTI (Isabel Briggs Myers): theory-based (Jung); 4 dichotomies: Extraversion/Introversion, Sensing/iNtuition, Thinking/Feeling, Judging/Perceiving; 16 four-letter types (e.g., ISFJ). Theory-based tests guided by a theory; factor-analytic tests derive factors from data.
confusable_with: Raymond B. Cattell = 16 PF and fluid/crystallized; James McKeen Cattell = coined 'mental test' — two different Cattells

back: Show vague/ambiguous stimuli to elicit unconscious projections. Three formats: (1) Association — 'What does this inkblot resemble?' (Rorschach: 10 cards); (2) Completion — complete incomplete sentences (Rotter ISB); (3) Construction — draw a person or make up a story (TAT: 31 cards, 20 used per client; ages 4+). Favored by psychodynamic clinicians. Clinical psychologists most trained; examiner bias is common risk.
confusable_with: Rorschach = inkblots (association); TAT = pictures (construction/narrative); Rotter ISB = incomplete sentences (completion)

front: Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (Bender Gestalt II)
back: Created by psychiatrist Lauretta Bender. Client copies 16 geometric figures. Primarily used to detect brain damage, neurological impairment, or motoric difficulties (also considered an expressive projective measure). Suitable for ages 4 and above. Used when a counselor suspects organic/neurological difficulty.
confusable_with: Bender is best known for neurological screening, not personality — unlike TAT/Rorschach which are purely projective personality measures

front: Interest inventories — age, limitations, and AARC
back: Best for high school age and above — interests not stable before then; fully stable around age 25. Key criticism: overemphasize professional/white-collar occupations, underrepresent blue-collar jobs. Important: interests and abilities are NOT highly correlated (e.g., someone may love music but have little skill). Advantages: least threatening type of test; high reliability for adults. AARC (Association for Assessment and Research in Counseling): ACA division focused on assessment.
confusable_with: Interest ≠ ability — high interest in music doesn't predict musical skill; do not confuse interest stability age (25) with Holland's theory

front: Social desirability vs. acquiescence vs. deviation in self-reports
back: Social desirability: client answers in what they believe is the socially acceptable/expected way. MMPI-2 lie scale controls for this via forced-choice items. Acquiescence: client always agrees regardless of content. Deviation: client deliberately gives unusual/extreme responses. All are response style biases that reduce validity of self-report measures.
confusable_with: Social desirability = wanting to look 'normal/good'; deviation = wanting to look unusual — both skew results away from truth

back: Assessment techniques without standardized administration or scoring procedures. Examples: checklists, diaries/journals, case notes, sociograms, clinical interviews, professional staffings, behavioral observations. Contrast with standardized tests (WAIS-IV, MMPI-2, GRE) which have specified administration/scoring guidelines and quantitative norms.
confusable_with: Informal ≠ invalid — informal assessments are ethically acceptable but cannot be compared to population norms

back: Proportion of test-takers who answer an item correctly: D = # correct / total tested. Range: 0.0 (nobody correct = impossible) to 1.0 (everyone correct = too easy). Ideal difficulty = .50 (50% correct, maximizes discrimination). For selective admission (e.g., top 25%), set difficulty at the selection rate (e.g., .25).
confusable_with: Higher difficulty INDEX = easier item (more people pass it) — counterintuitive; higher number = easier, not harder

front: Oscar K. Buros and the Mental Measurements Yearbook (MMY)
back: Oscar K. Buros: created the first major publication reviewing available psychological tests. The Mental Measurements Yearbook (MMY) contains professional reviews to help counselors select appropriate tests. After his death, the Buros Center at University of Nebraska continued this work. Counselors should consult MMY before selecting tests for clients.
confusable_with: Buros = test review resource; DSM = diagnostic manual; APA Ethics Code = professional guidelines — all guide practice but for different purposes

back: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA): persons 18 and older can inspect their own academic records (including test data) AND records of their minor children. Can demand correction of errors. Information cannot be released without adult consent. Applies to educational institutions receiving federal funding.
confusable_with: HIPAA governs medical/mental health records; FERPA governs educational records — different laws for different settings

front: Achievement vs. aptitude test — distinction and GRE special case
back: Achievement test: measures what has already been learned/mastered (NCE, licensing exams, classroom tests). Aptitude test: predicts potential for future learning or performance (SAT, GRE, GATB, MCAT, LSAT). KEY: predictive validity most important for aptitude tests. GRE = aptitude-achievement test (does both). School selection tests generally = aptitude.
confusable_with: NCE = achievement test (tests current knowledge); GRE = aptitude-achievement hybrid; SAT is commonly called aptitude but tests learned content too

back: Standardized test: has formal, specific procedures for administration and scoring; includes quantitative normative data for comparison. Nonstandardized: lacks procedural guidelines; no population norms. Both Stanford-Binet and Wechsler scales are standardized, individual tests requiring specific administration training.
confusable_with: Standardized ≠ objective — standardized describes administration/norming; objective describes scoring format

back: Two different versions of the same test that are interchangeable — each form must have the same mean, standard error, and statistical properties. Used to prevent test-retest practice effects. Counterbalancing is necessary when establishing parallel forms reliability (half get Form A first, half get Form B first).
confusable_with: Parallel forms reliability measures the equivalence of two versions; test-retest measures stability of one version over time

back: Assessment technique in which a client sorts cards with statements into piles ranging from 'most like me' to 'least like me.' Used by Carl Rogers to investigate personality and self-esteem: client creates an 'ideal self' profile that can be compared to their current self-perception. The larger the gap between ideal self and current self, the lower the self-esteem.
confusable_with: Q-Sort is associated with Rogers (person-centered), not with projective testing or the MMPI

front: DSM / ICD vs. CPT codes in psychological testing context
back: When third-party insurance payment is required, counselors may use psychological tests to support a DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual) or ICD (International Classification of Diseases) diagnosis. CPT (Current Procedural Terminology) codes tell insurance companies WHICH service was provided (e.g., individual therapy, group therapy) — NOT the diagnosis.
confusable_with: DSM/ICD = what the client has (diagnosis); CPT = what the counselor did (service/procedure) — different classification systems

front: Test use ethics: key principles for counselors
back: (1) Tests are a single source of data — not infallible; always explain limitations to clients. (2) Inform clients about test limitations before administering. (3) Involve client in test selection to improve cooperation. (4) Ethics violation to administer a test not normed on client's population. (5) Consult test manual to determine target population. (6) Consult MMY for professional test reviews. (7) Clinical psychologists most qualified for projective testing; social workers least trained.
confusable_with: Counselors should inform clients of limitations, NOT withhold test results — transparency is ethical; withholding = paternalistic
